Native American reservations [or Indian reservations; accept Standing Rock Indian Reservation]

The protagonist of this novel displays a copy of the Serenity Prayer in his office, mirroring a character who keeps it in a locket with a picture of her mother. A character in this novel tells the main character to "ask for Wild Bob" if he finds himself in Cody, Wyoming. The protagonist of this book tells Bernard O'Hare's wife that the novel he is writing will be called (*) The Children's Crusade. This novel's main character and Montana Wildhack are kidnapped by plunger-shaped aliens who live on the planet Tralfamadore. The firebombing of Dresden is relived by Billy Pilgrim while "unstuck in time" in, for 10 points, what novel written by Kurt Vonnegut?
Slaughterhouse-Five[or Slaughterhouse-Five: The Children's Crusade: A Duty-Dance with Death

In a play by this author, Time herself appears onstage to announce that 16 years have passed, and a lifelike statue of a king's long-dead wife miraculously comes to life. This author wrote a long and difficult-to-classify play about a Trojan love affair, Troilus and Cressida. A play by this author contains the amusing stage direction to "exit, pursued by a (*) bear." The villain of a play by this author demands a "pound of flesh" from Antonio. Plays by this author classified as "problem plays" include his Measure for Measure. This playwright wrote The Winter's Tale. For 10 points, what English playwright is often referred to as "the Bard"?

In the 1961 expansion draft, this team drafted a hall-of-fame dual-threat quarterback nicknamed "Scramblin' Fran." A player for this team pretended to moon Packers fans in what Joe Buck described as "a disgusting act." Under Bud Grant, this team lost 3 Super Bowls in the 1970s with Alan Page and the (*) "Purple People Eaters." A 2018 playoff game between this team and the Saints ended with an improbable touchdown by Stefon Diggs. This team's current elite wide receiver room features Jordan Addison and Justin Jefferson. For 10 points, name this NFC North team, the benefactors of the Minneapolis Miracle.

This organ produces albumin, which makes up 50% of the protein in plasma. This organ is the primary site of lipid droplets that store fat-soluble vitamins such as A and D. This organ secretes angio•tensinogen to regulate blood pressure. Macrophages in this organ known as Kupffer cells digest aging red blood cells to produce (*) bili•rubin. This organ receives blood from the gastrointestinal tract through the portal vein. This is the only human organ capable of full regeneration. This organ can develop cirrhosis in response to chronic alcohol consumption. For 10 points, name this large blood-filtering organ in the abdomen.

The last of a line of these people sent a message to Julian the Apostate lamenting that several springs had dried up. A group of these people called the Pleiades hung pots from trees at a grove in Dodona. Herodotus wrote that one of these people advised Croesus of Lydia that a "great empire would be destroyed" before his disastrous war with Persia. Prior to the Battle of Salamis, one of these people claimed that only (*) "wooden walls" would protect Athens. One of these people who would sit on a tripod and inhale gasses from volcanic faults was called the Pythia in honor of Apollo. For 10 points, name this sort of person who advised visitors to Delphi.

oracles [accept prophetesses or soothsayers or fortune tellers or augurs or seers; accept the Oracle of Delphi or the Delphic Oracle; accept Pythia until read; prompt on priests or priestesses; reject “sibyls”]

Musicians interact with each other using this practice by "trading fours" or "trading eights." This practice is used by accompanying rhythm section players in "comping." Musical notation for this practice is marked by an empty staff with slashes on every beat, sometimes annotated with chord symbols. The term "bebop" originates from another technique for this practice that employs (*) meaningless syllables. Ella Fitzgerald was known for her pioneering use of this practice when scat singing to fill in forgotten lyrics. For 10 points, name this practice performed by jazz musicians when constructing melodies on the spot during solos.

jazz improvisation [accept word forms such as improvising; accept blowing; prompt on composition or word forms such compose; prompt on scat singing or scatting before “scat singing”; prompt on soloing before “comping” with “Musicians perform what musical practice in those solos?”]

Two answers required.An event involving these two people is evoked by the first thunderword of James Joyce's Finnegans Wake, which opens midsentence by describing "riverrun past" a location named for these two people. Alquist proclaims the robots Helena and Primus to be new versions of these two people in the play R.U.R. These two people take "wandering steps and slow" on a (*) "solitary way" after they recognize each others' nudity for the first time. In a 1667 epic poem, one of these two people causes them both to be expelled by Michael after she eats an apple at the encouragement of a serpent. For 10 points, in John Milton's Paradise Lost, what man and woman are cast from Eden?

Ending a conflict in this country was the goal of the most recent Treaty of Jeddah. The support of one group in this country by the United Arab Emirates led Macklemore to cancel a concert in Dubai. Two factions in this country had originally worked together to depose Omar al-Bashir. A military force in this country absorbed the remnants of the Janjaweed militia under its leader, (*) Hemedti. This country has seen the massacre of Masalit people in its region of Darfur. This country's army, led by Abdel al-Burhan, is fighting the Rapid Support Forces. For 10 points, name this country whose ongoing civil war has included the Battle of Khartoum.
Sudan [or Republic of the Sudan or Jumhuriyah as-Sudan; accept Sudanese Civil War]

This artist depicted George and the Dragon in the first use of a shallow relief style called stiacciato. According to Vasari, this artist shouted "Speak, damn you!" at a statue of Habakkuk nicknamed for its pumpkin-like head, Zuccone("zuh-KOH-nay"). This artist's wood artworks include the Santa Croce Crucifix and The Penitent Magdalene. This artist was inspired by a statue of Marcus Aurelius to depict the mercenary (*) Erasmo da Narni in the equestrian statue Gattamelata. In the first freestanding male nude since antiquity, this artist sculpted a boy in a helmet resting one foot on a decapitated head. For 10 points, name this Renaissance sculptor of a bronze David.

Zoe Leonard scattered 295 sewn examples of these items across the floor in an installation at the Philadelphia Museum of Art. A Lawrence Beitler photo featuring a large crowd at the feet of Thomas Shipp and Abram Smith inspired a poem by Abel Meeropol titled for these objects.That poem was later popularized by a song named for these objects set in the "gallant south" that describes (*) "Blood on the leaves and blood at the root." These objects represent victims of lynching in that Billie Holliday song which describes them as "strange." For 10 points, name this general type of produce often grown in an orchard.

One type of these objects named for their strong magnetic field was suggested as a source for soft gamma repeaters. Another type of these objects can be used in a "timing array" to detect low frequency gravitational waves. Occasionally, these objects will "spin up," or increase in rotational speed, in an event called a "glitch." Those types of these objects regularly emit a (*) beam of radiation described by a lighthouse model. Magnetars and pulsars are examples of these objects, which like black holes are formed by supernovae. For 10 points, name these dense stellar objects made of a namesake uncharged particle.

Members of this religion try to balance an egg during a festival celebrating one of a trio of concepts this religion was the first to call the Three Treasures. Members of this religion may cover their right fist with their left hand at chest level to represent the "supreme ultimate." A series of stories, including a scholar dreaming of a (*) butterfly or imagining the butterfly is dreaming of him, were written by this religion's scholar Zhuangzi ("JWONG-dzuh"). The idea of "effortless action" or wu wei is central to this religion, whose central texts include the I Ching, which compares darkness and light to the yin and yang. For 10 points, Laozi ("LAO-tzuh") wrote the foundational text of what Chinese religion that follows "the Way?"

A third-generation form of this technique passes molecules through a nanopore such as alpha-hemolysin. Four kinds of fluorescent labels are used in a form of this technique developed by Illumina. Results from this technique can be "aligned" to existing data using the database BLAST ("blast"). A form of this technique that relies on chain-terminating (*) ddNTPs was developed by Frederick Sanger. The "shotgun" form of this technique, which divides chromosomes into small fragments, was used to map 3 billion letters during the Human Genome Project. For 10 points, name this technique that determines the order of nucleobases in DNA.
DNA sequencing [or gene sequencing or genome sequencing; accept Sanger sequencing, shotgun sequencing, Illumina dye sequencing, or nanopore sequencing]

Cecil Beaton forced the recall of a 1938 issue of this publication by inserting barely-legible slurs into the margins of an illustration. Along with Harper's Weekly, this publication was the longtime employer of Dovima with the Elephants photographer Richard Avedon. Karl Lagerfeld controversially served as the theme of the 2023 iteration of an event organized by this publication. In 2020, (*) Harry Styles appeared on the cover of this magazine in a dress. The staff of this magazine organize the Met Gala, including current editor-in-chief Anna Wintour. For 10 points, Conde Nast publishes what prominent fashion magazine named for a French term?

A man emulates this character's style of speech of asking then immediately answering questions when rewriting an article on Comrade Ogilvy. A man sheds "gin-scented" tears as he observes "the smile" under this character's "dark mustache" and realizes he had "won the victory over himself." People chant this character's initials as an "act of self-hypnosis" at the end of the (*) Two Minutes Hate. This character is defined as an undying "face on thetelescreen" in a book by Emmanuel Goldstein. Ingsoc ("ing-SOSCH") mottos such as "War is peace" appear on posters of this character's face seen by Winston Smith. For 10 points, name this figure who is "watching" in George Orwell's 1984.

This construct is fragmented in a "virtual" process in which the kernel manages this construct's hierarchy. In C, the free function releases this construct to the system, as part of a set of functions for managing this construct that includes malloc. CPU speed improvements are hindered by this construct's namesake (*) "wall," which is mitigated by using a cache. The non-volatile NAND ("nand") flash type of this construct is used in solid-state drives. This resource is sold in namesake "sticks" of 16 to 32 gigabytes. For 10 points, name this resource that stores information in a computer for random access.
memory [accept virtual memory, memory hierarchy, dynamic memory allocation, NAND flash memory, non-volatile memory, random-access memory, or RAM]

One of these particles and its antiparticle were discovered independently by two scientists in an event called the "November Revolution." In 2003, the Belle Experiment found X(3872) ("X 3-8-7-2"), which might be made of four of these particles. The first of these particles was discovered at SLAC ("slack") using deep inelastic scattering. These particles may have fractional charges such as (*) +2/3 or -1/3, and they cannot be separated due to color confinement. These particles are bound together by gluons, which mediate the strong force. Protons and neutrons are made up of, for 10 points, what particles that come in six "flavors" including up and down?

The Goldroad was built by an "Old King" from this family who called the Great Council of Harrenhal. Dunk's squire Egg was secretly a member of this purple-eyed family, who later put down the Fourth Blackfyre Rebellion. A queen from this family who liberated the Slaver Cities of Meereen and Yunkai had earlier married (*) Khal Drogo of the Dothraki Horde. Alicent Hightower backed the Greens against Princess Rhaenyra's ("ray-NEAR-a") Blacks in a civil war amongst this family called the Dance of the Dragons. This Valyrian family's first ruler, Aegon the Conqueror, forged the Iron Throne. For 10 points, Daenerys ("deh-NAIR-ees") is a member of what royal family in Game of Thrones?
Targaryens [accept House Targaryen or the Targaryen dynasty; accept Jaehaerys I Targaryen, Aegon V Targaryen, Daenerys Targaryen, Rhaenyra Targaryen, or Aegon I Targaryen]

A phrase from this language meaning "know the ways" titles a work that contains an illustration of a cosmic egg engulfed in flames, which represents God. An author who wrote in this language described his method as "faith seeking understanding" and discussed a being greater than all that may be conceived in the Proslogion. A work written in this language proposes arguments from "the unmoved mover" and "first cause" as part of (*) five ways of proving God's existence. This non-vernacular language was the lingua franca in European academia until the 1700s. For 10 points, Thomas Aquinas wrote the Summa Theologica in what dead language?
Latin (The first line describes Scivias, which is by Hildegard of Bingen. The Proslogion is by Saint Anselm.)

The speaker of a poem set in this state accompanies her Aunt Consuelo to a dentist appointment and reads National Geographic in the waiting room. An aquarium in this state "stands in a Sahara of snow now" according to the poem "For the Union Dead." After seeing a "gleam of light" in a (*) "belfry-tower," a character in a poem set in this state "springs to the saddle." That character instructs a friend to hang "one [lantern] if by land, and two if by sea" in a church in this state to alert him to the approach of the British. For 10 points, what U.S. state is the setting of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's "Paul Revere's Ride"?
Massachusetts [or MA] (The first poem is Elizabeth Bishop’s “In the Waiting Room.”)

A governor of this state funded a capitol building featuring a 450-foot tall art deco tower. A governor of this state who had an affair with stripper Blaze Starr was known as Uncle Earl. A plan to eliminate dust storms was detailed by a book written in this state that proposed appointing Franklin Roosevelt as Secretary of the Navy. That book written in this state advocated for a wealth cap and is titled (*) My First Days in the White House. This state's Depression-era governor used the slogan "Every Man a King" to promote his "Share Our Wealth" program before his 1935 assassination. For 10 points, Huey Long governed what state from Baton Rouge?

The 2004 Foreshore and Seabed act contested these people's ownership of coastal areas. A Caren Fox-chaired tribunal created in 1975 investigates breaches of a treaty signed by these people whose text translated "sovereignty" as a word for "governance." A flagstaff in the Bay of Islands was cut down by a leader of these people, (*) Hone Heke ("hoh-nay hek-ay"). These people's iwi fought in the Musket Wars. In 1840, these people's rangatira and William Hobson signed the Treaty of Waitangi. Five of these people's dedicated electorates are on the North Island, including one in greater Auckland. For 10 points, name these indigenous people of New Zealand.

It's not a scherzo, but a Tchaikovsky work in this genre begins with the solo violin playing "long G, long A" before an ascending up-bow staccato run ending on six down-bow A's. A piece in this genre named for a garland precedes the "Rose Adagio" in Sleeping Beauty. The 5/4 second movement of the "Pathetique" Symphony is nicknamed for a (*) "limping" example of this genre. A harp cadenza opens a work in this genre "of the Flowers" often extracted from The Nutcracker. Johann Strauss II was dubbed "king" of this genre that includes his "Tales from the Vienna Woods" and "The Blue Danube." For 10 points, name this genre of triple-meter ballroom dance.
waltz [or valse; accept Valse-Scherzo; accept “limping waltz”; accept “The Garland Waltz” or Sleeping Beauty waltz; accept “Waltz of the Flowers”; accept “The Blue Danube Waltz”]

While working for this organization, Ralph Bunche claimed that if a certain objective failed he would break plates over his colleague's heads. Former president Harry Truman insinuated that the 1961 death of a leader of this organization prior to meeting Moise Tshombe to discuss the Congo Crisis was an assassination. (*) Dag Hammarskjold led this organization, which ordered Israel to withdraw from territories acquired during the Six-Day War in Resolution 242. In 1971, China assumed Taiwan's permanent seat on this organization's Security Council. For 10 points, name this international body that succeeded the League of Nations.
United Nations [or UN; accept United Nations Security Council or UN Security Council] (The objective from the first line is the 1949 Egypt-Israel negotiations)

It's not in North America, but people in this country have reported seeing hoop snakes, or snakes that roll around in the shape of a circle. In a story from this country, an eel makes a frog laugh and spit out all the water of the land. A creature from this country usually described as a large seal or swimming dog is the bunyip. A person can navigate this country by knowing the words to a (*) "songline." Anthropological studies of this country's mythology center on a period called "The Dreaming" or "Dreamtime." For 10 points, the Rainbow Serpent features in several stories from what country's Aboriginal people?

Agents of this empire staged a kidnapping of a man who was later hidden at Wartburg Castle. This empire's free imperial cities avoided subordination to territorial princes and were represented directly in the Imperial Diet. This empire's Great Interregnum was ended by the ascent of Charles IV of Luxembourg. Mikhail Kutuzov's defeat at a frozen lake led (*) Francis II to dissolve this empire, which lasted for almost one thousand years and was later dubbed the First Reich. For 10 points, name this large confederation of Germanic states that, despite its name, was not led from Italy.
Holy Roman Empire [or the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation or HRE or Sacrum Imperium Romanum or Heiliges Römisches Reich; accept the First Reich before read]

This work contains a group of semi-nude figures called The Acrobats that may be similar to the Twelve Metal Colossi. A National Geographic project employed purple made from barium copper silicate and white made from fired bone to reconstruct the coloration of this work. Tests of the soil around this work lent credence to the idea that it was once adjacent to 100 (*) rivers of mercury. In 1974, Yang Zhifa's attempt to dig a well led to the discovery of this work, which is still partially underground in the city of Xi'an ("shee-AHN"). For 10 points, a type of fired clay names what massive collection of soldiers that guarded the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang?

Terracotta Army [or the Terracotta Soldiers or the Terracotta Warriors; accept any answer that indicates the terracotta sculptures from Qín Shǐ Huáng’s tomb; accept Shǐ Huáng Dì or Qín Shǐ Huáng Dì or the First Qin Emperor in place of “Qín Shǐ Huáng”; prompt on Qín Shǐ Huáng’s tomb] (Barium copper silicate is used to produce Han purple and Han blue.)

An early form of this food named oxygala was usually consumed with honey, while a Mongolian version of this food is called tarag. This food is used as a main ingredient in the Indian dish raita, as well as in Indian marinades due to tenderizing enzymes present in it. This food is the primary ingredient in a sauce that combines it with (*) cucumbers, garlic, and herbs; that sauce is often served with gyros ("YEE-rows") and is called tzatziki ("zaht-ZEE-key"). This food can be strained to produce its "Greek" variety. For 10 points, name this food, a fermented milk product that may come packaged with "fruit on the bottom," produced in America by companies like Chobani and Yoplait.
yogurt [accept Greek yogurt; accept dahi or mosaru or thayir or perugu; prompt on curd by asking “what is another name for that food?”]

The rate at which this quantity changes with temperature equals the constant-pressure heat capacity. This quantity is defined as the internal energy plus pressure times volume. This quantity is held constant while a gas is throttled through a valve, known as Joule-Thompson expansion. This quantity for a reaction, plus temperature times (*) entropy, equals the Gibbs free energy. Changes in this quantity can be summed across all components of a reaction according to Hess's law. The change in this quantity determines if a reaction is endothermic or exothermic. For 10 points, name this thermodynamic state function symbolized H.

A nonfiction book by this author names Huckleberry Finn as the source of all modern American literature during a digression from its Tanzanian setting. This author published Green Hills of Africa while living in Key West at a house now home to a population of polydactyl cats. A novel by this author in which characters like Lady Brett Ashley attend (*) bullfights popularized Gertrude Stein's idea of the"Lost Generation." This author boosted his public image as an outdoorsman by writing a novella in which an eighty-four day streak of bad luck is broken when Santiago catches a marlin. For 10 points, name this author of The Old Man and the Sea.
Ernest Hemingway [or Ernest Miller Hemingway] (Lady Brett Ashley is the love interest of Jake Barnes, the narrator of The Sun Also Rises.)

A service on this holiday may include singing the Improperia, or Solemn Reproaches. On the day before this holiday, many Episcopal Churches host an Agape ("uh-GAHP-ay") Meal whose liturgy concludes with the stripping of the altar. On this holiday, Simon of Cyrene ("sy-REE-nee") and Veronica are commemorated with devotional icons placed around a church. A service on this holiday is called the (*) Three Hours Agony. This holiday's events are depicted through the Stations of the Cross. Services on this holiday include the Seven Last Words from the Cross and other events during the Passion. For 10 points, what holiday celebrated two days prior to Easter commemorates the crucifixion of Jesus?

A character in this novel recounts a dream about swimming in a lake where "there is no monster...just water." This novel's protagonist is surprised when his friend falsely admits to stealing money and a watch. This novel's protagonist witnesses a public stoning in a soccer stadium while trying to rescue his nephew, Sohrab. A character in this novel repeats the phrase (*) "for you, a thousand times over." After winning a tournament in which this novel's title objects are adorned with glass shards, the protagonist watches Assef sexually assault his Hazara friend. The Afghan children Amir and Hassan drift apart in, for 10 points, what novel by Khaled Hosseini?

An electrically conductive phase of this element is thought to be responsible for Jupiter and Saturn's magnetic fields. The 21 centimeter line radiated by this element during the Dark Ages can be observed redshifted in radio astronomy. Lyman-alpha forests are spectral lines created by this element. The red emission of this element's first (*) Balmer line gives nebulae their color. This element is consumed by both the CNO ("C-N-O") cycle and the proton-proton chain. The interstellar medium is mostly composed of this element. Main sequence stars fuse this element into helium. For 10 points, name this most abundant element of the universe.

A man with this profession describes his role as a "custodian of our peace of mind" before mentioning how white people feel uncomfortable with Uncle Tom's Cabin. A spoof on an annual tradition in which people with this profession mock poetry causes a woman to cry to a reading of "Dover Beach." A salamander patch distinguishes people with this profession, who are assisted by a massive eight-legged (*) dog called the Mechanical Hound. A man with this profession kills Captain Beatty and escapes his city after encountering the open-minded Clarisse. For 10 points, Guy Montag has what profession that destroys books in Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451?

firemen [or fireman; accept firefighters; prompt on book-burners by asking “what title do book-burners have in that novel?”] (In the novel, every building is fireproof, so firefighters were turned into the force of the state as firemen.)

At this location, Thaddeus Lowe's aircraft Enterprise failed to properly identify itself and was forced down behind enemy lines. A unit nicknamed for their black headgear withstood an enemy assault at John Brawner's orchard near this location. A John Pope defeat at this site led to the Army of Virginia's dissolution. Irvin McDowell's troops (*) retreated during a battle at this site where one general was described as "standing like astone wall." Families from nearby Washington, D.C. picnicked at this site while viewing the first major battle after the Fort Sumter bombardment. For 10 points, name this Virginia site of two Civil War battles.
Bull Run [or Manassas, Virginia; accept the First or Second Battles of Bull Run or Battle of First or Second Manassas] (Thaddeus Lowe was the leader of the short-lived Union Army Balloon Corps.)

A king of this city received a new name after being rescued from slavery by Heracles, and used to be called Podarces. A baby born in this city became frightened when seeing his father with his helmet on. The river Scamander flowed near this city. Near this city, both Aphrodite and Ares were wounded by a (*) warrior who was given divine sight by Athena named Diomedes. A prince of this city's corpse was dragged behind a chariot around this city 12 times, after which his father Priam came to ransom his dead body. For 10 points, Hector was a prince of what city, the setting of the Iliad?

Twelve boxes made of this material are organized vertically in Untitled (Stack), a work typical of minimalist artist Donald Judd. The term "plop art" was used to insult Tilted Arc, a 120-foot-long sculpture by Richard Serra made of this material. This material was used in Mountains and Clouds, which unusually does not feature its artist's namesake (*) red. Chicago's Federal Plaza is home to a 53-foot tall work made from this material called Flamingo. Wires suspend pieces of this material in Lobster Trap and Fish Tail, a mobile by Alexander Calder. For 10 points, name this type of common sculptural medium, such as iron.

A line from this poem titles an essay collection that examines the lost children of the Haight-Ashbury District by Joan Didion. This poem contrasts "passionate intensity" of the "worst" to a "lack of conviction" by the "best." "Twenty centuries of stony sleep" in this poem are "vexed to nightmare by a rocking cradle." "A (*) "blood-dimmed tide" in this poem is evoked by its exclamation that "the falcon can not hear the falconer" in a world chaotic like a "widening gyre." This poem ends with the image of a "rough beast" who "Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born." For 10 points, name this poem about the Biblical apocalypse by W.B. Yeats ("yates").

A nationalist narrative sometimes credited with inventing this conflict claims that mozarabs suffered under the rule of this conflict's eventual losing side. This conflict began following the establishment of the Kingdom of Asturias by a Visigoth named Pelagius. States called taifas formed during this conflict after the collapse of the last Umayyad state. The folk hero and knight (*) El Cid fought for the ruler of Zaragoza during this conflict. The defeat of the Emirate of Granada by the forces of Ferdinand and Isabella is often marked as the 1492 end of this conflict. For 10 points, name this long conflict in which Christian kingdoms ended Muslim rule in the Iberian Peninsula.

In a play in this language, a character dies from a botched abortion after being assaulted by Melchior in a hayloft. The main character of a play in this language narrowly escapes execution when a messenger arrives to pardon him and make him baron, and earlier married Polly Peachum. A play in this language was adapted into the Broadway musical Spring Awakening. A "play with music" in this language is termed "an (*) opera for beggars" and features Mack the Knife. A poem written in this language was set to music in Beethoven's 9th symphony. For 10 points, The Threepenny Opera and "Ode to Joy" are works in what language used by Bertolt Brecht and Friedrich Schiller?

A first movement clarinet motif in a work by this composer in the rhythm [read slowly] "quarter, quarter, eighth-eighth-eighth-eighth, quarter" interrupts a trombone solo. A hymn whose melody begins [read slowly]"quarter notes G, G, up to C, eighth notes C, D, E, C" is the basis of a theme and variations in a ballet by this composer. A ballet by this composer includes (*) "Corral Nocturne" and "Saturday Night Waltz." This composer quoted the shaker hymn "Simple Gifts" in a ballet choreographed by Martha Graham that bookended another ballet with "Buckaroo Holiday" and "Hoe-Down." For 10 points, name this American composer of Rodeo and Appalachian Spring.

This scientist proposed that electricity and magnetism were both caused by the "electrodynamic molecule," a precursor to the idea of the electron. This scientist's "force law" governs the attraction or repulsion caused by the magnetic fields of two parallel wires. A law named for this scientist states that the line integral of the magnetic field around a (*) closed path is proportional to the current enclosed. A displacement current term was added by James Maxwell to that law named for this scientist, who also names a unit equal to one coulomb per second. For 10 points, what French physicist names the SI unit of current?
André-Marie Ampère [accept Ampere’s law or Ampere’s circuital law or Ampere’s force law]

A museum dedicated to this island's taxis contains one that was clipped by the wing of an ATR 72 that crashed on takeoff from Songshan Airport. A codeword used to begin Pearl Harbor referenced this island's tallest mountain, known as Mount Jade. To counteract gusts of wind, four floors of a building on this island are partly dedicated to a tuned mass damper. That building on this island preceded the (*) Burj Khalifa as the world's tallest building and is named for its 101 floors. Tapioca pearls and milk tea make up boba, a drink that originated on this island. For 10 points, name this island, once known as Formosa, that contains Taipei.
Taiwan [accept Formosa before mention; accept Republic of China or ROC; reject “China” or “People’s Republic of China”]

In this country, a computerized economic planning system called Project Cybersyn was developed. In Operation Colombo, this country's DINA secret police disappeared many dissidents. Singer Victor Jara was tortured and murdered in a sports stadium following a coup in this country. After giving a radio speech in this country, a leader was found dead holding an AK-47 in (*) La Moneda Palace. Milton Friedman educated a group of economic advisors in this country dubbed the "Chicago Boys." A 1973 coup in this country overthrew Salvador Allende. For 10 points, name this country formerly led by Augusto Pinochet.
Chile [or the Republic of Chile or República de Chile]

A proposed expansion of this conference nicknamed the "Airplane Conference" preceded it becoming the AAWU. A rivalry game between teams in this conference ended with a kickoff return touchdown while the band prematurely ran onto the field. In 2023, this conference's champion was led by Heisman finalist (*) Michael Penix ("PEN-nicks") Jr., and lost to Michigan in the College Football National Championship. A 2023 suit gave Washington State and Oregon State sole ownership of this conference. For 10 points, name this NCAA sports conference that saw a mass exodus of teams in 2024, named for the ocean on the USA's west coast.
the Pac-12 [accept the Pacific Coast Conference, the Big Five, the Big Six, the Pacific-8, the Pac-8, the Pacific-10, or the Pac-10]

An experiment by this researcher relied on "connectors" who would reach a clothing merchant named Mr. Jacobs. This researcher asked subjects to replicate the speech of a radio signal in an experiment inspired by the play Cyrano de Bergerac. This psychologist tested the average path length of social networks in an experiment in which people in Omaha or Wichita forwarded (*) mail to someone in Boston. Participants in a Yale University experiment by this psychologist were encouraged to continue punishing a "learner" who claimed he had a heart condition.
